dossier.architecture: Telescoping low-pivot arm adapted from 2910 2023, with arm-powered climb.

subsystems.drivetrain: Swerve and lengthened wheelbase to stabilize taller arm.
subsystems.intake: Wide arm-mounted roller intake collects arbitrary-orientation coral; aluminum funnels center it. Same mechanism handles algae.
subsystems.transfer: Shared end effector avoids handoff between separate acquisition and scoring mechanisms.
subsystems.scoring: Four-motor shoulder and two-motor extending arm; stages lengthened about three inches for L4/net reach.
subsystems.endgame: Post-week-5 powered cage wheels/latches replaced slower between-poles clamp. Arm provides lift; servo ratchet holds shoulder after disable.
subsystems.controls: Two Limelight 4s provide field localization and pose alignment; separate CAN buses discussed in interview.

versions: Arm extended relative to prior-year implementation, forcing chassis change.
Week-5-to-Worlds cage capture replaced; shoulder ratchet added during build development.

context_documents.title: 2025-359 · A telescoping arm avoids a handoff but moves a large work envelope
context_documents.body:
# 2025-359: A telescoping arm avoids a handoff but moves a large work envelope

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

The interview describes four shoulder motors with a stated 111:1 reduction, a chain-driven dead-axis pivot, and a two-motor telescoping arm. Its wide collector uses front/back roller groups and aluminum centering guides to acquire differently oriented coral; rigid guide plates reflect coral’s low compressibility. The retained record describes extending stage length for L4/net reach.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team links the multi-motor shoulder to power demand. Its acquisition geometry is intended to bring floor coral into the same mechanism that scores it, avoiding a separate transfer.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

Eliminating a handoff trades transfer risk for arm inertia, sweep clearance and control burden. Extension changes both shoulder torque and the position of the robot’s loaded center of mass. A floor hard stop can define a repeatable pickup plane, but should not be confused with clearance throughout the rest of the motion. Thin coral tolerates less forced compression than foam fuel, so roller selection must be paired with a controlled guide gap.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Map shoulder current and deflection through extension, test pickup against a wall, and verify coral control during acceleration and sudden chassis braking.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

## Sources and navigation

- [https://youtu.be/AFthn6GQme4](https://youtu.be/AFthn6GQme4)

source_reviews.title: FRC Team 359 2025 Robot Pic Reveal
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team reveal and opened robot photograph
facts: Team credits 2910 Phantom arm lineage, lists a 26 by 33 in low-offset SDS L3+ swerve, 106 lb, floor and station coral, all four levels, both algae destinations and deep cage.
limitations: Reveal claims establish intended capability, not event reliability or hidden geometry.

source_reviews.title: 359 reveal discussion, mechanism revisions
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team replies and opened extension and cage images
facts: Wrist angle and broadside coral caused misses. Week 1 extension slipped under high drive. Chain replaced the outer extension belt, with an inner belt retained. Wider IGUS and a printed guide addressed routing near the added climber.
limitations: Team practice and event reports, with no load traces, build drawings or complete event serial history.

source_reviews.title: 359 reveal discussion, early climb and auto
facts: Team describes three L4 pieces from three sources and active cage hooks chosen to cope with cage movement.
limitations: Linked videos were not used as evidence.

subsystems.name: Coral acquisition and wrist
subsystems.construction: Arm-mounted pickup and belt-driven wrist. Team reports additional tensioners for the wrist belts.
subsystems.operation: Present the tool to the floor or feeder, retain the piece through arm motion and release at the reef.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team reported that angled floor coral was easier to grab and that incorrect wrist angle made acquisition harder.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Pickup tolerance should be plotted against both tube angle and lateral offset. Driver translation may turn a missed entry into capture while lengthening the cycle.
subsystems.interfaces: Wrist position affects roller-to-carpet and tube-to-tool contact. Telescope and shoulder set the gross scoring pose.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check belt preload and wrist reference after nose strikes. The reported broadside miss is a real acquisition boundary.
subsystems.unknowns: Wheel spacing, sensor logic and station receiving geometry.

subsystems.name: Arm extension and chassis
subsystems.construction: The 2910-derived mechanism retains an internal extension belt. 359 replaced the outer belt with chain using a WCP spline adapter for the pinion sprocket.
subsystems.operation: Shoulder and telescope carry the tool to branches, including L3 and L4. Team says it capped extension to roughly 50–60 percent power early to avoid slipping.
subsystems.team_rationale: Team attributes extension speed limits to longer reach and intake weight, and reports better operation after the chain retrofit.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A slip that changes actual tool travel relative to feedback can appear as inconsistent placement. Positive drive can restore usable acceleration while introducing tension, lash and shock-load considerations.
subsystems.interfaces: Arm reaction feeds the base through the pivot. The wired tool moves with the telescope.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Track chain tension, sprocket retention, stage synchronization and physical versus reported extension after a jam.
subsystems.unknowns: Reductions, hard stops and telescope sensor arrangement.

subsystems.name: Deep cage capture and moving wiring
subsystems.construction: Early active hooks. Later 2910-assisted clamp inspired by 368, plus a wider IGUS carrier and printed guide where the added hardware crosses the carrier path.
subsystems.operation: Acquire the cage, then lift through the arm package. Team reported about 1.5 seconds from contact to deep climb in practice for the newer clamp.
subsystems.team_rationale: Team considered passive capture quicker but less dependable on a moving cage. Additional wiring needed wider carrier links.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Test capture separately from proof loading and power-off holding. A missed cage and a lost load after contact have different remedies.
subsystems.interfaces: Cage load enters the arm and chassis. The assembly shares a moving clearance boundary with the cable guide.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Inspect guide wear, carrier snag points, cage engagement and positive load holding after service.
subsystems.unknowns: Exact latch geometry, retention under disable and event deployment timeline.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: The Hawaiian Kids adapted the 2910 Phantom telescoping arm family to carry a coral tool through floor acquisition and elevated reef placement. The arm swings relative to a low chassis mount, extends for reach, and carries a wrist whose floor angle is adjustable. The team reports both station and floor supply, scoring at every coral level, and both algae destinations. The mechanism also supports the cage apparatus, so upgrades to extension, wiring and cage engagement interact even though they address different phases of the match.
source_review.piece_flow: Floor coral enters the arm-tip pickup when the tool is presented at the pickup angle. The team reports that driving into a piece can salvage some imperfect approaches, although a tube broadside to the intake was troublesome. The arm moves the held coral into the scoring envelope and the tool releases at the target. Station pickup supplies an alternative route into the scoring cycle. The published sources establish algae acquisition and both release destinations but leave algae contact geometry and net release settings open.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: The base was published as 26 by 33 inches with low-offset SDS L3+ swerve. A change in arm angle changes both reach and height, while telescope extension and wrist angle add control over the tool pose. The cage device sits above the arm and shares space with the moving wiring carrier. Engineering implication: test clearance with the cable at its widest displaced position and with all cage hardware fitted. A clean CAD centerline would not bound the real harness sweep.
revisions: Week 1 belt restriction, March 5 practice-bot outer-chain conversion, later-event improvement reported retrospectively, and April practice-bot cage clamp prepared for Champs. Internal extension and wrist belts remained according to the May clarification.
transferable_principles: Keep a reused arm’s geometry and its new load case separate. Verify extension at loaded scoring angles, measure pickup acceptance over random coral orientations, and cycle the full cable harness after any add-on.
disconfirming_conditions: A heavier tip, a different wheel footprint, repeated broadside floor supply, or an unreliable power-off hold can remove the value of a compact shared arm despite successful stationary placement.
remaining_gaps: Interview captions were unavailable in this pass. Motor counts, calibration logic, detailed algae contact, full competition installation history and comparative cycle data remain open.
recommended_images: Post 63, IMG_4324 for the extension revision discussion.
Post 67, IMG_5229 for cage hardware context. Use the accompanying team text for version attribution.
